title: Is Node.js is a language or framework?

content.text: Node.js is not a language or a framework, but rather a JavaScript Runtime Environment that allows developers to run JavaScript outside the browser.
Open source, server-side JavaScript runtime.
Allows you to run JavaScript on your machine or on servers.
Built on the V8 JavaScript engine for speed.
Robust ecosystem with npm.
Node is all about Modules.
Open-Source means that the source code of Node.js is publicly available.
View: You can see how Node.js is built under the hood.
Modify: If you want to customize or improve Node.js, you can do it.
Contribute: Developers around the world actively contribute to improve Node.js.
Cross Platform means Node.js can run on multiple operating systems without needing major changes.
Windows, MacOS, Linux
JavaScript Runtime Environment refers to the environment where your JavaScript code runs.
JavaScript typically runs in the browser (like Chrome or Firefox) to handle frontend tasks.
Node.js allows JavaScript to run outside the browser, on the server.
It provides tools to interact with the server, like:
File system (read/write files)
Network (handles HTTP requests)
Database (connect to database like MongoDB or MySQL)

title: Why Node.js Special as a Runtime?

content.text: Node.js uses Google Chrome V8 Engine to compile JavaScript into machine code, making it lightning fast.
Node.js comes with Built-in APIs (like fs for file systems or http for servers) so you can build powerful applications without extra libraries.
Single Language for Full Stack Development:
Developers can use JavaScript for both frontend and backend, reducing complexity.
For example, a MERN Stack Project (like MongoDB, Express, React, Node).
High Performance:
Thanks, to the V8 engine, Node.js is super fast.
It can handle thousands of simultaneous connection with ease.
Event-Driven and Non-Blocking I/O:
Unlike traditional servers that block a thread for each request, Node.js uses an asynchronous model, making it highly efficient for handling multiple tasks.
Scalable for modern applications:
Ideal for real-time applications like chat apps, streaming platforms or online games.
It stands for Read-Eval-Print Loop or Read, Evaluate, Print and Loop. It's an interactive programming environment that allows you to execute JavaScript code one statement at a time.
You can open your terminal and use node command.
You can use it to taste simple JavaScript code similar to browser devtools.
CRTL + C to exit out of it.
Each part of the acronym highlights a specific step in how the REPL works:
Read: The REPL read the user's input (a single line or multiple line of code) and parses it to a data structure that JavaScript engine can understand.
Eval (Evaluate): The parsed input is evaluated (executed) by JavaScript engine. If the input is a valid expression, the REPL computes the result.
Print: The result of the evaluated expression is printed on the console so the user can see the output.
Loop: The process then loops back, waiting for the input, and continues until the user exits.
In Node.js there is no window or document. Why? Because Node.js runs outside the browser - it doesn't deal with the DOM or browser-specific APIs.
Instead, Node.js has a global object. It's the equivalent of window in the browser but designed for a server-side environment.
globalThis is a new feature introduced in ECMAScript 2020 (ES11) that provides a standard way to access the global object in any JavaScript environment.
What is it useful?
In the past, accessing the global object varied depending on the environment:
Browser: window
Node.js: global
Web Workers: self
Other Environments: Might have there own global objects
Self-contained code unit:
Each file in a Noe.js is treated as a separate file.
Variables, functions or objects defined in one file are not accessible by another file by default unless you explicitly export them.
Node.js uses the commons module system (module.exports for export and require for import) to ensure the code in one file does not pollute or interfere with the global scope.
This makes your code modular, maintainable and easier to debug.
console.log(add(5, 10));      // Output: 15

title: Named and Aggregate Exports and Imports.

content.text: Avoid mixing module.exports and exports.property incorrectly. If you reassign module.exports, it will override any exports.property assignment.
Use consistent syntax for clarity:
Assign everything at once with module.exports = {...};
Eg: module.exports = {add, sub, multi, div};
Or assign properties individually with module.exports.property.
Eg: module.exports.add; module.exports.sub; modules.exports.multi;
Also while import:
Assign everything at once like const {...} = require('./math');
Or assign in a variable like const math = require('./math') and use method to apply the function.
Eg: const {add, sub, multi, div} = require('./math');
Eg: const math = require('./math'); // math.add, math.sub, math.multi, math.div

The fs (File System) module in Node.js is a core module that allows you to work with the file system, enabling you to read, write, update, delete, and watch files.
Writes content to the file. If the file does not exist, it creates one.
Syntax: fs.writeFileSync(filePath, data, options)
Reads the content of the file asynchronously and logs it.
Syntax: const data = fs.readFileSync(filePath, options)
Appends new content to the file without overwriting the existing content.
Syntax: fs.appendFileSync(filePath, data, options)
Deletes the file completely.
Syntax: fs.unlinkSync(filePath)
Renames a file from one name to another.
Syntax: fs.renameSync(oldPath, newPath)
Writes data to a file, replacing the file if it already exists.
Syntax: fs.writeFile(path, data, options, callback)
Reads the contents of a file asynchronously and returns the data as a buffer or string.
Syntax: fs.readFile(path, options, callback)
Appends data to a file. If the file doesn’t exist, it is created.
Syntax: fs.appendFile(path, data, options, callback)
Deletes a file asynchronously.
Syntax: fs.unlink(path, callback)
Rename a file asynchronously.
Syntax: fs.unlink(oldPath, newPath, callback)
Creates or overwrites a file with specified content.
Syntax: fs.promises.writeFile(path, data, options).then('File created.').catch()
The readFile() method reads data from a file.
Syntax: fs.promises.readFile(path, options).then((data) => console.log(data)).catch((err) => console.error(err))
The appendFile() method adds content without overwriting the existing data.
syntax: fs.promises.appendFile(path, data, options).then('File updated.').catch()
The unlink() method removes the specified file asynchronously.
Syntax: fs.promises.unlink(path).then().catch()

content.text: Writes data to a file asynchronously. If the file exists, it overwrites the content.

Syntax: fsPromises.readFile(path, options)
Adds content to the end of a file. If the file does not exist, it creates a new one.

title: Advantages and Use Cases of FS Module.

content.text: No need for manual callbacks.
Cleaner and more intuitive asynchronous workflows using async/await.
Suitable for modern JavaScript applications.
Reading Files asynchronously in a non-blocking way.
Writing or Appending Data to files without blocking the event loop.
Performing Multiple File Operations sequentially or concurrently with promise chaining.
Handling Errors Gracefully with .catch() or try...catch blocks.
